compatibility.newFormatPolicy: Add definitions and fixtures using these operations; no engine edit is required for supported compositions. New primitive operations require explicit interpreter capability versions.

normalizedNodes.coordinates: Keep physical source row/column plus rowspan/colspan origin; expanded cells reference the original source span.

input.recognitionFeatures: Derived from roleRules, node relationships and source text; never from a format-specific engine branch.

expressionLanguage.pathSyntax: dot-separated own-property path; numeric array indices allowed; no wildcards, function calls, prototype properties or executable text
expressionLanguage.all: mismatch if any operand mismatches; otherwise unresolved if any unknown; otherwise match
expressionLanguage.any: match if any operand matches; otherwise unresolved if any unknown; otherwise mismatch

pipelineExecution.parameterBinding: First resolve defaults.processingParameters[format.mode], merge local processing.parameters using defaults.mergeRule, then replace objects having exactly one parameter key. Reject missing parameters; never evaluate strings as code.
pipelineExecution.stageInputs: label.nodes or previous named stage output
pipelineExecution.bindings: Role and grammar references are resolved before tokenization/grouping; each captured value retains its original source span.
pipelineExecution.constraintIteration: When candidate.constraints is present and empty, the patient filter matches. When absent, invalid, incompletely parsed or carrying an unknown axis, it is unresolved. Otherwise evaluate every constraint with its own field/metric/unit; combine using all.
pipelineExecution.fieldAssembly: project uses mappings and source-bound roles/tokens; a missing required field remains null/unresolved, never borrowed from a sibling branch.

featureDerivation.roles: Match roleRules against local and ancestor headers, keeping evidence; count matching roles per table.
featureDerivation.inferredHeaderRoles: true only when a unique two-column indication/regimen interpretation satisfies the format bindings without conflicting numeric source headers.
featureDerivation.componentCount: count distinct source-identified component names, not dose token count.

contextMatching.matchScope: same source-bound section/row/column or explicit source relation
contextMatching.negativeScopePrecedence: exclude or unresolved, never positive substring match
contextMatching.organismIdentity: exact canonical species when label is species-specific

fieldBinding.metadataFallbackSource: retrieved label.identity fields, with source identity evidence
fieldBinding.oneHeaderMayBindMultipleRoles: retain all supported roles; contradictory binding is unresolved
fieldBinding.headerUnitInheritance: only unique source-bound header unit in same row/column lineage
fieldBinding.sharedPhaseSequence: group all required phases before emit

contract.regexDialect: ECMAScript regular expressions, compiled from pattern/flags fields; regular-expression objects are never serialized as executable code.

route.code: canonical route scalar from source/metadata; never guess a route

typedRanges.missingEndpoint: unbounded only if explicitly source-supported; unparsed endpoint is unresolved

definitions.label: Cockcroft–Gault (source lean/ideal weight)

requirements.message: Cockcroft–Gault requires serum creatinine at steady state. Enter CrCl separately when that requirement is not met.
This equation is enabled for adults only.
Age must be below the formula constant 140.
This estimator is not used for a dialysis profile.
Adefovir specifies Cockcroft–Gault using lean or ideal body weight. Supply that weight and basis; total profile weight is not substituted.

definitions.displayEquation: CrCl = source-required lean or ideal weight (kg) × (140 − age) / [72 × serum creatinine (mg/dL)]; multiply by 0.85 for the female equation.

definitions.label: Cockcroft–Gault

requirements.message: Cockcroft–Gault requires serum creatinine at steady state. Enter CrCl separately when that requirement is not met.
This equation is enabled for adults only.
Age must be below the formula constant 140.
This estimator is not used for a dialysis profile.

definitions.displayEquation: CrCl = weight (kg) × (140 − age) / [72 × serum creatinine (mg/dL)]; multiply by 0.85 for the female equation.

definitions.label: Cefdinir label pediatric indexed CrCl (historical K × height / creatinine)

requirements.message: The sampled pediatric cefdinir dosing label starts at 6 months.
This equation option is scoped to the sampled pediatric label (through age 12 years).
A positive height or body length in centimeters is required.
Serum creatinine in mg/dL must be positive.
A steady-state creatinine is required; do not use this estimate in a non-steady-state profile.
This estimate is not used for a dialysis profile.

definitions.displayEquation: Indexed CrCl = K × height/body length (cm) / serum creatinine (mg/dL), in mL/min/1.73 m². The cefdinir label specifies K = 0.55 for children older than 1 year and K = 0.45 up to 1 year. This is the historical source equation, not a substitution for another eGFR equation or adult CrCl.

diseases.label: Bacteremia & Endocarditis
diseases.note: S. aureus Bacteremia (SAB) / Endocarditis: Mandatory echocardiography and repeat blood cultures. Never use Daptomycin for pneumonia.

diseases.label: Osteomyelitis & Septic Arthritis
diseases.note: Vertebral / Long-Bone Osteomyelitis: Requires 4–6 weeks of parenteral or highly bioavailable oral therapy.

diseases.label: Necrotizing / Hospital Pneumonia
diseases.note: MRSA HAP/VAP or Post-Influenza Pneumonia: Treat with IV Vancomycin or Linezolid.

diseases.label: Impetigo

diseases.label: All E. coli Presentations
diseases.note: Predominant facultative Gram-negative rod in urinary, hepatobiliary, and intra-abdominal infections.

diseases.label: Uncomplicated Cystitis / Lower UTI

diseases.label: Pyelonephritis / Urosepsis
diseases.note: Pyelonephritis / urinary-source sepsis: use a systemic agent guided by severity and susceptibility. Nitrofurantoin is not suitable for renal-parenchymal infection.

diseases.label: Intra-Abdominal Infection / Peritonitis
diseases.note: Use systemic enteric Gram-negative coverage; add anaerobic coverage when the syndrome/source requires it. Source control is central.

diseases.label: Cholangitis / Biliary Infection
diseases.note: Biliary infection: systemic enteric Gram-negative coverage plus source control/biliary drainage when indicated; tailor to cultures.

diseases.label: Pyogenic Liver Abscess
diseases.note: Drainage/source control and cultures are central; select systemic therapy by likely mixed flora and susceptibility results.

diseases.label: Source-listed cUTI / Pyelonephritis
diseases.note: This label index does not establish a urosepsis regimen; susceptible organisms and product eligibility remain required.

diseases.label: All Pseudomonas Presentations
diseases.note: Non-fermenting Gram-negative rod with intrinsic resistance to Ceftriaxone, Ertapenem, Aminopenicillins, and Tetracyclines.

diseases.label: HAP / Ventilator Pneumonia
diseases.note: Select susceptible antipseudomonal therapy using the source and clinical context. Ciprofloxacin and Levofloxacin have systemic label branches. Aminoglycosides require monitoring and are not standalone HAP/VAP therapy.

diseases.label: Complicated UTI / Pyelonephritis
diseases.note: Pseudomonal UTI: Ciprofloxacin/Levofloxacin or IV Cefepime/Ceftazidime/Aminoglycoside.

diseases.label: Malignant Otitis Externa / Osteomyelitis
diseases.note: Skull-Base / Foot Puncture Osteomyelitis: High-dose Ciprofloxacin or IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam for 6 weeks.

diseases.label: Osteomyelitis / Bone and Joint Infection
diseases.note: Ciprofloxacin bone/joint FDA source row. The combined older bone/ear presentation remains available; this selection is specific to bone infection.

diseases.label: All Klebsiella Presentations
diseases.note: Intrinsically resistant to Ampicillin/Amoxicillin (chromosomal SHV-1 beta-lactamase).

diseases.label: Necrotizing Pneumonia / HAP
diseases.note: Pulmonary infection: select an active systemic agent according to susceptibility; carbapenems are generally reserved for resistant organisms.

diseases.label: Complicated UTI / Pyelonephritis
diseases.note: Complicated UTI / renal-parenchymal infection: choose a systemic agent according to susceptibility and severity. Nitrofurantoin is not suitable for pyelonephritis.

diseases.label: Pyogenic Liver Abscess
diseases.note: Pyogenic liver abscess requires imaging, drainage when indicated, cultures, and susceptibility-directed systemic antibiotics.

diseases.label: All Pneumococcal Presentations
diseases.note: Leading cause of CAP, acute otitis media, sinusitis, and adult bacterial meningitis.

diseases.label: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
diseases.note: Pneumococcal Pneumonia: High-dose Amoxicillin, Ceftriaxone, or Respiratory Fluoroquinolone.

diseases.label: Bacterial Meningitis
diseases.note: Pneumococcal Meningitis: Empiric Ceftriaxone 2g IV Q12H + Vancomycin + Dexamethasone.

diseases.label: Otitis Media & Sinusitis
diseases.note: Acute Otitis Media / Sinusitis: Amoxicillin or Amoxicillin/Clavulanate.

diseases.label: All Group A Strep Presentations
diseases.note: Universally susceptible to Beta-Lactams. In necrotizing fasciitis/toxic shock, add Clindamycin or Linezolid for exotoxin suppression.

diseases.label: Pharyngitis / Tonsillitis
diseases.note: Guideline options are not ranked by FDA card order: oral Penicillin V or Amoxicillin for 10 days are preferred oral regimens; benzathine Penicillin G by IM injection as a single dose is also a guideline-listed option (adult dose 1.2 million units; pediatric dosing is weight-based). Macrolides are alternatives for selected penicillin-allergic patients; resistance varies.

diseases.label: Erysipelas / Cellulitis
diseases.note: Streptococcal nonpurulent skin infection. The IV penicillin and cefazolin cards show separately attributed IDSA adult references. Necrotizing fasciitis has its own presentation and combination pathway.

diseases.label: Documented GAS Necrotizing Fasciitis
diseases.note: Urgent surgical management plus intravenous Penicillin G and Clindamycin. The two components are not monotherapy alternatives.

diseases.label: Rheumatic Fever Prophylaxis

diseases.label: Acute Meningitis & Meningococcemia

diseases.label: Close-Contact Chemoprophylaxis

Community-Acquired Pneumonia.note: Adult educational overview. Outpatient vs inpatient status, comorbidities, severity, local resistance, and MRSA/Pseudomonas risk determine the regimen; this is not a patient-specific empiric protocol.

Nosocomial / Ventilator Pneumonia.note: Use local antibiogram, prior cultures, severity, and validated MRSA/Pseudomonas risk to select and narrow therapy.

Bacterial Meningitis.note: Empiric coverage depends on age, immune status, pregnancy, Listeria risk, and local resistance; this is not a complete empiric regimen.

Brain Abscess.note: Drainage, neurosurgical context, immune status, prior surgery, and cultures determine therapy. This map is an organism-oriented overview, not a complete regimen.

Infective Endocarditis.note: Regimens depend on native vs prosthetic valve, acuity, organism, and susceptibility; culture-directed therapy is essential.

Bacteremia / Septicemia.note: Blood cultures, source, severity, resistance risks, and source control determine treatment; this is an organism map, not a universal sepsis regimen.

Osteomyelitis (Acute / Chronic).note: Obtain cultures when feasible; therapy depends on site, hardware, chronicity, source control, and susceptibility.

Septic Arthritis.note: Joint aspiration and drainage are central; selection depends on Gram stain, cultures, age, and gonococcal risk.

Acute Pyelonephritis.note: Use urine culture and local susceptibility. Nitrofurantoin and oral fosfomycin are not suitable for renal parenchymal infection.

Complicated / Uncomplicated UTI.note: Cystitis and pyelonephritis are different syndromes. Nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin apply to selected lower-tract infection, not systemic or renal-parenchymal infection.

Acute Bacterial Prostatitis.note: Urine culture, severity, urinary retention, prostatic penetration, and local fluoroquinolone resistance determine selection; nitrofurantoin is not a prostatitis treatment.

Cellulitis & Skin Structure.note: Purulence, systemic toxicity, exposure, and MRSA risk change coverage; abscesses require drainage when indicated.

Intra-Abdominal Infection / Peritonitis.note: Coverage is usually polymicrobial and must include enteric Gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes when indicated. Source control and local resistance are central; fluoroquinolones require local susceptibility support. Routine empiric Candida coverage is not recommended for community-acquired infection.

Pyogenic Liver Abscess.note: Imaging, drainage/source control, cultures, and susceptibility-directed systemic therapy are central. Coverage depends on community vs healthcare acquisition and local resistance; this is not a fixed empiric regimen.

Diabetic Foot Infection.note: Severity, ischemia, necrosis, prior antibiotics, MRSA risk, Pseudomonas risk, and need for debridement/source control determine breadth. Not every case needs broad-spectrum therapy.

Acute Cholecystitis / Cholangitis.note: Enteric Gram-negative bacilli predominate; add anaerobic or enterococcal coverage according to anatomy, severity, and healthcare-associated risk.

Clostridioides difficile Colitis.note: Fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin are the principal options for most episodes. Metronidazole is not listed as routine stand-alone therapy; fulminant disease requires a separate specialist-guided regimen.

Febrile Neutropenia.note: Prompt risk assessment and antipseudomonal therapy are required; add Gram-positive coverage only for specific indications and tailor to cultures/local resistance.

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease.note: Combination therapy should account for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes; this organism map is not a complete regimen.

Gonorrhea.note: Ceftriaxone is the recommended backbone; add chlamydia treatment when coinfection has not been excluded, per current guidance.

Chlamydia trachomatis.note: Doxycycline is generally preferred for uncomplicated infection in nonpregnant adults; pregnancy requires a different regimen.

Pulmonary Tuberculosis.note: Active drug-susceptible TB requires combination therapy. The listed agents are components of a multidrug regimen, not alternatives or monotherapy; susceptibility results and current TB guidance are essential.

Invasive Candidiasis.note: Species, susceptibility, severity, prior azole exposure, and source control determine selection.

Invasive Aspergillosis.note: Treatment depends on species, susceptibility, host factors, and drug interactions.

Acute Bacterial Sinusitis.note: Typical bacterial targets are S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and M. catarrhalis; many cases do not require antibiotics.

Acute Otitis Media.note: Common bacterial pathogens are S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and M. catarrhalis; age and local recommendations affect management.

Streptococcal Pharyngitis.note: Group A Streptococcus is the principal bacterial target; confirm the diagnosis before treatment.

Syphilis.note: Penicillin formulation and duration depend on stage and neurologic/ocular involvement; do not interchange regimens.

Neurosyphilis.note: Requires a CNS-penetrating penicillin regimen; do not substitute routine early-syphilis regimens.

Helicobacter pylori.note: Eradication is combination therapy; clarithromycin-containing regimens depend on susceptibility and local resistance.

Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection.note: These oral options require the specific label indication and susceptibility. This uncomplicated context does not establish suitability for pyelonephritis or complicated UTI.

Esophageal Candidiasis.note: Caspofungin has a distinct esophageal-candidiasis regimen; do not import the loading dose from another indication.

Typhoid Fever.note: Chloramphenicol is restricted by its serious toxicity and source indication. This index is not a treatment preference or support for the carrier state.

MEROPENEM.adjustedDose: 500 mg – 1 g IV every 12 hours (if CrCl 10–25 mL/min); 500 mg IV every 24 hours (if CrCl < 10 mL/min)
MEROPENEM.contraNote: Accumulation risk: Unadjusted doses in eGFR < 30 increase risk of beta-lactam neurotoxicity and seizures.

IMIPENEM.adjustedDose: 250 mg – 500 mg IV every 8–12 hours (if CrCl 15–29 mL/min)
IMIPENEM.contraNote: High CNS Seizure Risk in eGFR < 30 (especially if CrCl < 15 mL/min or CNS lesions); prefer Meropenem.

ERTAPENEM.adjustedDose: 500 mg IV/IM every 24 hours (50% dose reduction when CrCl < 30 mL/min)
ERTAPENEM.contraNote: Renally cleared: Must reduce standard 1 g daily dose to 500 mg daily when eGFR < 30 mL/min.

CEFEPIME.adjustedDose: 1 g IV every 12 hours (or 2 g IV every 24 hours for severe/febrile neutropenia if CrCl 11–29 mL/min)
CEFEPIME.contraNote: Relative Contraindication if unadjusted: Crosses blood-brain barrier in renal failure causing encephalopathy, myoclonus, and non-convulsive status epilepticus.

CEFTRIAXONE.adjustedDose: 1 g – 2 g IV every 24 hours (NO renal dose adjustment required; dual hepatic/biliary + renal excretion)
CEFTRIAXONE.contraNote: Safe in eGFR < 30 without dose reduction (cap maximum daily dose at 2 g/day in combined hepatorenal failure).

CEFAZOLIN.adjustedDose: 500 mg – 1 g IV every 12 hours (if CrCl 11–34 mL/min); 500 mg every 24h (if CrCl <= 10 mL/min)
CEFAZOLIN.contraNote: Primarily excreted unchanged in urine; extend interval to Q12H–Q24H when eGFR < 30.

PIPERACILLIN.adjustedDose: 2.25 g IV every 6 hours (or 3.375 g IV every 8 hours for nosocomial pneumonia if CrCl 20–40 mL/min; every 8–12h if CrCl < 20)
PIPERACILLIN.contraNote: High risk of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) if co-administered with Vancomycin; adjust maintenance dose for CrCl < 40 mL/min.

AMOXICILLIN.adjustedDose: 500 mg PO/IV every 12 hours (if eGFR 10–30 mL/min); 500 mg every 24 hours (if eGFR < 10 mL/min)
AMOXICILLIN.contraNote: Avoid 875 mg high-dose tablets in eGFR < 30; extend interval to Q12H to prevent crystalluria.

AMPICILLIN.adjustedDose: 1 g – 2 g IV every 8–12 hours (if CrCl 10–30 mL/min)
AMPICILLIN.contraNote: Extend dosing interval in eGFR < 30 mL/min.

PENICILLIN.adjustedDose: Reduce maintenance dose by 25–50% or extend interval to every 6–8 hours when CrCl < 30 mL/min
PENICILLIN.contraNote: High-dose IV Penicillin G in renal failure causes CNS neurotoxicity/seizures and electrolyte load.

CLOXACILLIN.adjustedDose: 500 mg – 2 g IV/PO every 6 hours (NO routine renal dose adjustment required; dual hepatic + renal clearance)
CLOXACILLIN.contraNote: Cleared substantially via hepatic metabolism and biliary excretion; standard dosing maintained in eGFR < 30.

OXACILLIN.adjustedDose: 1 g – 2 g IV every 4–6 hours (NO routine renal dose adjustment required)
OXACILLIN.contraNote: Hepatobiliary elimination predominates; no dose reduction needed in renal impairment.

NAFCILLIN.adjustedDose: 1 g – 2 g IV every 4–6 hours (NO renal dose adjustment required)
NAFCILLIN.contraNote: Cleared primarily by hepatic/biliary route; safe in eGFR < 30 without dose reduction.

DICLOXACILLIN.adjustedDose: 250 mg – 500 mg PO every 6 hours (NO renal dose adjustment required)
DICLOXACILLIN.contraNote: Hepatic and renal excretion; no dosage adjustment needed in renal insufficiency.

VANCOMYCIN.adjustedDose: Loading dose 20–25 mg/kg IV x1, then maintenance dosed strictly by Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM / AUC 400–600)
VANCOMYCIN.contraNote: Direct proximal tubular nephrotoxicity. Mandatory serum level monitoring in eGFR < 30.

GENTAMICIN.adjustedDose: Avoid routine use if possible; if essential, give single loading dose (3–5 mg/kg) and redose ONLY by serum trough (<1 mcg/mL)
GENTAMICIN.contraNote: High risk of irreversible vestibulocochlear ototoxicity and acute tubular necrosis (ATN) in eGFR < 30 mL/min.

AMIKACIN.adjustedDose: Initial loading dose 12–15 mg/kg IV, then extend interval (Q24–48H) strictly guided by serum drug levels
AMIKACIN.contraNote: Potent nephrotoxin and auditory ototoxin; avoid in eGFR < 30 unless no safer Gram-negative alternative exists.

PLAZOMICIN.adjustedDose: 10 mg/kg IV every 24 hours (if CrCl 30–59); 10 mg/kg IV every 48 hours (if CrCl 15–29 mL/min)
PLAZOMICIN.contraNote: Aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; monitor trough levels and CrCl closely.

AMPHOTERICIN B.adjustedDose: Prefer Liposomal formulation (3–5 mg/kg IV daily); pre-hydrate with 500 mL 0.9% NaCl and monitor K+ / Mg2+ daily
AMPHOTERICIN B.contraNote: Causes afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, distal renal tubular acidosis (RTA), and K+/Mg2+ wasting.

ANIDULAFUNGIN.adjustedDose: 200 mg IV loading dose on Day 1, then 100 mg IV daily (NO renal dose adjustment required)
ANIDULAFUNGIN.contraNote: Cleared by non-enzymatic chemical degradation; 100% safe in severe renal failure.

LINEZOLID.adjustedDose: 600 mg IV/PO every 12 hours (NO primary renal dose adjustment, but monitor platelets closely)
LINEZOLID.contraNote: Two primary oxidation metabolites accumulate 7-to-8-fold in eGFR < 30, increasing risk of thrombocytopenia.

DAPTOMYCIN.adjustedDose: 4–6 mg/kg IV every 48 hours (extend interval from Q24H to Q48H when CrCl < 30 mL/min)
DAPTOMYCIN.contraNote: Must extend dosing to every 48 hours in CrCl < 30 mL/min and monitor CPK twice weekly.

CIPROFLOXACIN.adjustedDose: 250–500 mg PO every 12–18 hours OR 200–400 mg IV every 18–24 hours (if CrCl < 30 mL/min)
CIPROFLOXACIN.contraNote: 50–70% excreted renally; reduce dose or extend interval in eGFR < 30.

LEVOFLOXACIN.adjustedDose: 750 mg initial dose, then 500 mg every 48 hours (if CrCl 20–49); OR 500 mg initial, then 250 mg every 48 hours (if CrCl 10–19)
LEVOFLOXACIN.contraNote: Substantially excreted unchanged in urine; requires Q48H maintenance frequency when eGFR < 30.

MOXIFLOXACIN.adjustedDose: 400 mg PO/IV every 24 hours (NO renal dose adjustment required)
MOXIFLOXACIN.contraLevel: RENAL SAFE (DO NOT USE FOR UTI)
MOXIFLOXACIN.contraNote: Hepatic/biliary clearance requires no renal dose adjustment, but achieves poor urinary concentrations.

GATIFLOXACIN.adjustedDose: 400 mg initial dose, then 200 mg every 24 hours when CrCl < 40 mL/min
GATIFLOXACIN.contraNote: Renally cleared fluoroquinolone; high risk of severe hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia in renal insufficiency.

DOXYCYCLINE.adjustedDose: 100 mg PO/IV every 12 hours (NO renal dose adjustment required)
DOXYCYCLINE.contraNote: Excreted via GI tract chelation (unlike other tetracyclines); safe in eGFR < 30.

TETRACYCLINE.contraNote: Anti-anabolic effect markedly increases BUN, hyperphosphatemia, and acidosis in renal impairment.

NITROFURANTOIN.contraNote: Fails to reach therapeutic urinary concentrations in eGFR < 30 while systemic accumulation causes neuropathy and pulmonary toxicity.

SULFAMETHOXAZOLE.adjustedDose: Reduce dose by 50% (if CrCl 15–30 mL/min); AVOID if CrCl < 15 mL/min
SULFAMETHOXAZOLE.contraNote: Trimethoprim blocks ENaC channels in collecting duct, causing hyperkalemia and crystalluria in eGFR < 30.

CLARITHROMYCIN.adjustedDose: 250 mg PO twice daily (or 500 mg once daily) — 50% dose reduction required when CrCl < 30 mL/min
CLARITHROMYCIN.contraNote: Renal clearance drops sharply below CrCl 30 mL/min, increasing QTc prolongation risk.

AZITHROMYCIN.adjustedDose: 500 mg Day 1, then 250 mg–500 mg daily (NO routine renal dose adjustment)
AZITHROMYCIN.contraNote: Primarily biliary excretion; no dosage adjustment needed in mild-to-moderate renal failure.

CLINDAMYCIN.adjustedDose: 600 mg – 900 mg IV every 8 hours or 300–450 mg PO QID (NO renal dose adjustment required)
CLINDAMYCIN.contraNote: Hepatically metabolized with minimal renal excretion (<10%); safe in eGFR < 30.

CIPROFLOXACIN: CrCl 30–50: reduced oral dosing range per FDA label; adjust IV accordingly.
CEFEPIME: CrCl 30–60: dose reduction required (FDA label); neurotoxicity risk if unadjusted.
MEROPENEM: CrCl 26–50: recommended dose given q12h (FDA label).
IMIPENEM: Dose reduction per FDA label table when CrCl <90; seizure risk.
PIPERACILLIN: CrCl 20–40: reduced dose per FDA label; AKI risk with vancomycin.
NITROFURANTOIN: FDA label lists CrCl <60 as a contraindication (guidelines tolerate ≥30 — clinical judgment).
SULFAMETHOXAZOLE: No adjustment at CrCl >30 mL/min (FDA label); monitor K⁺ and creatinine.
ERTAPENEM: No adjustment at CrCl >30 mL/min (FDA label).
DAPTOMYCIN: No adjustment at CrCl ≥30 mL/min (FDA label).

records.text: Source contraindication: CrCl ≤55 mL/min, serum creatinine >1.5 mg/dL, or urine protein ≥100 mg/dL. A lower-dose table must not override this exclusion.
A rise in serum creatinine changes or stops the maintenance regimen. The unchanged 5 mg/kg branch is withheld; review the exact source adjustment and proteinuria requirements.
Moderate hepatic impairment uses a separate maintenance branch; loading-dose applicability remains indication-specific.
An interacting enzyme inducer changes the source regimen. Do not reuse the unadjusted esophageal branch.
Retinal or visual-field changes exclude the routine prophylaxis branch; inspect the full source contraindications.
A previous serious quinolone/fluoroquinolone reaction requires an alternative and source review before further systemic use.
Systemic fluoroquinolones can worsen myasthenia gravis; the routine source regimen is withheld when this history is supplied.
Systemic ciprofloxacin with tizanidine is contraindicated. The ordinary dose is withheld; local formulations require their own product review.
This label does not recommend either formulation when eGFR is below 15 mL/min/1.73 m², including hemodialysis. CrCl is not this metric.
Sampled nitrofurantoin product-label contraindication: CrCl below 60 mL/min. Do not replace it with a guideline threshold or an eGFR value.
IV use only. Probenecid and saline prehydration are required; renal eligibility, proteinuria and phase must be supplied before a regimen is matched.
Serious marrow toxicity; blood counts and concentration monitoring. The retrieved record places dosing in an unclassified section, which the current dosing adapter does not import.
Confirm chloroquine susceptibility and geography. Salt and base quantities are different; severe malaria and liver-stage eradication are not covered by a weekly prophylaxis dose.
CrCl, augmented clearance and CRRT effluent have separate source branches; confirm the applicable renal metric and infusion duration.
Source cautions include bleeding/hypoprothrombinemia and an alcohol interaction.
Oral axetil tablets/suspension and injectable cefuroxime are formulation-specific; oral formulations are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.
Systemic macrolide products: inspect product-specific QT, hepatic and interacting-medicine restrictions. Local ophthalmic/topical products have different exposure and instructions.

Do not combine with fluoropyrimidines (including fluorouracil, capecitabine, tegafur or flucytosine). At least 4 weeks must elapse after brivudine before a fluoropyrimidine. Check the full contraindications.

Systemic products: myelosuppression, fetal/reproductive toxicity and renal adjustment. Induction, maintenance and transplant prevention are separate source branches; ophthalmic ganciclovir is a different product.

Requires product-label clearance in mL/min/kg even when serum creatinine is normal, plus weight, indication/phase, hydration, electrolyte monitoring and a controlled IV infusion. Unindexed CrCl/eGFR cannot substitute.
CMV prevention in eligible transplant recipients; not active CMV disease treatment. Cyclosporine changes dosing; recipient/serostatus, age, weight, formulation and timing must match the source.

Refractory post-transplant CMV only. Avoid ganciclovir/valganciclovir coadministration. Anticonvulsants or rifabutin can change the source dose; other inducer and immunosuppressant interactions require review.

ORLYNVAH is a fixed combination for eligible adult women with uncomplicated UTI and limited or no alternative oral options. Not a pyelonephritis/cUTI substitute; preserve probenecid restrictions and renal eligibility.
Preserve the 3:1 component ratio, loading/maintenance sequence, source renal band, 3-hour infusion and timing after hemodialysis. The US cIAI indication requires concurrent metronidazole.
Systemic products: check source-specific renal adjustments, hydration and neurotoxicity risks. Oral, IV, buccal and topical products cannot exchange regimens.
Immediate-release, IV and local products are distinct; no transfer of renal bands between formulations.
The 750, 500 and 250 mg baseline regimens have different renal sequences; preserve the complete sequence and source indication.
Systemic and ophthalmic products are distinct. Systemic moxifloxacin is not a UTI or reliable Pseudomonas treatment.
Oral, ophthalmic and otic products have separate indications. Historical gonorrhea label dosing does not establish current guideline suitability.
Renal dosing uses indexed eGFR, not CrCl: the IV and oral branches differ. The MRSA indication is ABSSSI; do not extend it to MRSA pneumonia.
Regional oral product. The archived US FACTIVE label is a source reference, not evidence of current US marketing or a live FDA API result.
AIFA authorised/marketed oral packages. Observe current fluoroquinolone restrictions and the local product information.
PEFLOXACIN LAROPHARM human oral product in the Romanian nomenclature. International insert is not imported by the FDA live-dose adapter.
AIFA authorised/marketed oral packages. Prulifloxacin is a prodrug; ulifloxacin is not an independently interchangeable product.
AIFA authorised/marketed MONOS oral package. Local product information is required for dosing.
Current Japanese local eye/ear product information. This evidence does not establish continued systemic lomefloxacin marketing.
Separate Japanese adult tablets, pediatric tablets/granules and ophthalmic products. Pediatric approval is indication/product-specific.
Japanese oral product; local susceptibility and source-specific renal instructions remain necessary.
Japanese tablets and IV product have different product information. Do not infer an IV regimen from an oral strength.
Japanese IV product. No FDA live-label dosing fallback is supplied for this international insert.
Regional oral product. The Korean insurance listing records a 2025 deletion; continued Korean supply is not asserted. Current regional availability and local product information must be checked.
Manufacturer human Zabolante product. Salt mass and active-moiety mass are different; no conversion is inferred.
IV parent drug. Oral alalevonadifloxacin is a separate prodrug product; do not substitute milligram amounts.
Oral prodrug of levonadifloxacin. Preserve the product-specific active-moiety equivalence and instructions.
Ophthalmic suspension only in the verified US source; do not use as systemic therapy.
Verified current US products are ophthalmic. Existing legacy CAP/sinusitis navigation links are retained for compatibility; they are not current US systemic-product evidence.
Verified finished XTORO otic product in the FDA NDC listing; this does not imply universal commercial supply or systemic use.
Topical human skin products. Local skin indications do not support systemic therapy.
Regional human product source; discontinued US systemic products do not establish current US availability. QT and phototoxicity risks require local label review.
NMPA 2026 human injection regulatory record. It establishes a regional human-product record, not FDA approval or a stock guarantee.
Regional human-product record; contemporary package availability is not fully verified. No live-dose fallback or current US marketing claim.
Chinese human originator/reference-product record. No FDA source adapter exists for the regional product insert.
Fixed otic combination; preserve both components and concentration. Not an ophthalmic or systemic product.
Fixed otic combination; the suspension is not interchangeable with ciprofloxacin monotherapy.
Fixed otic combination; both components and the exact product indication are retained.
Ophthalmic fixed combination after cataract surgery; do not substitute for a systemic or uncomplicated conjunctivitis regimen.
Combination HIV therapy only. Review lactic acidosis/hepatotoxicity, neuropathy, hematologic toxicity and product-specific renal/weight branches. Do not combine stavudine with zidovudine.
US source product is IM-only. Renal function, ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity and source monitoring limits matter; TB requires combination therapy.
Preserve loading doses, trough monitoring and maintenance adjustment from day 4. Oral C. difficile treatment differs from systemic products. The linked SmPC is a reference, not retrieved FDA dosing.
TDF and TAF are different prodrugs and doses. Confirm exact product, indication, HIV/HBV testing, renal/dialysis status and liver eligibility; stopping HBV therapy can cause severe exacerbation.
Oral nail therapy requires liver assessment; chronic or active liver disease is a contraindication. Fingernail and toenail courses differ.
Take with food. Avoid alcohol during treatment and for 3 days afterward; review pregnancy, breastfeeding interruption, partner treatment and indication-specific age/weight limits.

Velpatasvir is used in complete fixed combinations. Check HBV reactivation, acid-reducing medicines, amiodarone and other interactions. Cirrhosis, prior therapy, genotype and ribavirin requirements must match the product.
Inhaled powder via DISKHALER only; do not nebulize or inject. Check bronchospasm/airway disease, lactose/milk-protein allergy, age, symptom timing and treatment versus prophylaxis.
WHO/CDC reference for selected first-stage rhodesiense HAT: test dose, stage/CSF eligibility, age/weight, serial IV doses and renal/proteinuria monitoring. No FDA regimen is claimed.
Nitroimidazole: source alcohol/propylene-glycol and disulfiram restrictions; warfarin interaction; neuropathy and hepatic/dialysis instructions remain product-specific.
Infuse over one hour. Indication and age/weight branches differ; observed mean trial duration is not a fixed prescribed course. Monitor hepatic/renal/hematological effects.
Buccal, topical and vaginal products are distinct. Buccal tablet must not be crushed, chewed or swallowed; warfarin interaction and local administration instructions apply.
The sampled 2% ointment is topical only, for up to ten days; reassess absent response at 3–5 days. Not intranasal, ophthalmic or other mucosal use.
Oral absorption can cause nephrotoxicity, permanent ototoxicity and neuromuscular blockade. Bowel preparation is a combination/timing regimen; hepatic-coma daily totals are not single doses.
Serious hepatic and skin toxicity. Preserve 14-day lead-in, rash/escalation and restart-after-interruption instructions; combination ART only. Child-Pugh B/C and PEP exclusions apply.
LAMPIT source is pediatric, including term newborn ≥2.5 kg, with a 60-day weight/tablet schedule. Avoid alcohol; pregnancy testing/contraception and neuropsychiatric precautions apply.

PAXLOVID components must be coadministered. Complete CYP3A interaction review; source eGFR and severe renal day-1/day-2–5 sequences differ. Do not substitute indexed eGFR into a differently specified metric.
Take with food. This tablet source is for age ≥12; do not substitute its 500-mg tablet for pediatric suspension doses. Efficacy in HIV/immunodeficient patients has not been established.

Macrobid and macrocrystals have different schedules. Sampled labels contraindicate CrCl <60 mL/min and term/labor use; lower-UTI source only, not pyelonephritis. Guidelines with different thresholds are separate references.
Oral tablets, mouth-retained suspension and skin products are distinct. Preserve volume/activity equivalents and post-resolution course qualifications; not systemic treatment.

Raw FDA SPL available but harmonized UI metadata absent. Source age ≥12/weight ≥30 kg, pregnancy exclusion, contraception, Sjögren-Larsson exclusion and renal/hepatic monitoring apply; not a live-card availability claim.

FDA EUA fact sheet, not an FDA-approved drug label. Adult early high-risk COVID-19 only when alternatives are inaccessible/inappropriate. Raw FDA metadata lacks the harmonized fields needed by the current UI.

WHO/CDC intestinal tapeworm reference. Niclosamide is not available for human use in the United States; no compatible live WHO/CDC dosing adapter is supplied. Do not use this context for neurocysticercosis.
Fluoroquinolone boxed warnings and source renal thresholds apply. The sampled IV nosocomial-pneumonia indication excludes Pseudomonas; do not infer a label indication from general organism coverage.
Clarithromycin and its companion proton-pump inhibitor doses must not be confused. Source QT/CYP3A, renal/boosted-ART, hepatic and coronary-disease precautions apply.
Source severity and formulation differ; historical IV maxima are not routine regimens. Boxed C. difficile warning and source infusion limits apply.
Leprosy combination therapy only for the selected label branch. GI deposition/toxicity, QT risk, discoloration and source pregnancy testing require review; US access is restricted.
Lozenges dissolve slowly in the mouth. Skin, vaginal and troche products are distinct; the troche source is not systemic fungal therapy.

All sampled colistimethate doses are colistin base activity, not mass of the prodrug or international units. Obesity requires source-appropriate ideal weight; nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity and IV split-dose instructions apply.
This sampled generic source uses a single dose and 30-minute IV infusion. CrCl <30 without regular HD differs from regular HD; do not mix it with another product’s two-dose option.
Initial dermatitis-herpetiformis dosing is not maintenance titration or leprosy treatment. Review G6PD, anemia/hemolysis, methemoglobinemia, blood counts and hepatic precautions.
Skin and bloodstream doses differ. Not indicated for pneumonia or left-sided S. aureus endocarditis; source CK/myopathy, statin, eosinophilic-pneumonia and after-HD instructions apply.
PREZISTA must be taken with the correct ritonavir booster, food and other ART. Resistance, pregnancy, pediatric formulation, sulfonamide, hepatic and CYP3A conditions remain source-specific.
The source adult daily total is divided into two or four doses. Renal/hepatic impairment needs individualized reduction; no unverified fraction or interval is computed. This is not an SIADH regimen.

Adult severity columns are distinct from pediatric mg/kg/day. Oral therapy is not initial treatment of life-threatening infection; empty-stomach/water administration and susceptible-staphylococcus restrictions apply.
INSTI resistance and source-listed inducers change the interval. TIVICAY and TIVICAY PD are not mg-for-mg substitutable; ART, interactions and cation separation require review.

Use with other ART and the source resistance/treatment-history eligibility. Rifabutin changes dosing; strong CYP3A inducers are contraindicated. PIFELTRO is not the fixed-combination DELSTRIGO product.
Keep the named indication and source treatment/prophylaxis phase. Pediatric malaria dosing must not appear in an adult chlamydial regimen; pregnancy, cations and esophageal precautions apply.

Historical DailyMed capsule label; no current harmonized openFDA product was retrieved. Do not imply current US availability or first-line ART. Renal/weight/TDF branches, pancreatitis, lactic acidosis and contraindicated combinations require the exact archived source.

CDC reference only: confirm syndrome, age, quantitative Loa loa testing and onchocerciasis exclusion. Individual DEC treatment is distinct from mass drug administration; the unchanged app has no live CDC dosing-card adapter.
Source HLA-B*5701 screening, prior hypersensitivity, combination ART and hepatic restrictions apply. Never rechallenge after suspected abacavir hypersensitivity.

Source renal intervals require stable baseline CrCl. Cockcroft–Gault uses lean or ideal weight; total profile weight is not substituted. HIV screening, renal monitoring and post-discontinuation HBV flare precautions apply.
Neurocysticercosis and hydatid cycles differ. Preserve food, weight/daily maximum, steroid/anticonvulsant review and pregnancy/retinal/hepatic/blood-count monitoring.

Conventional divided dosing requires source peak/trough and renal/auditory/vestibular monitoring and daily maximums. The serum-creatinine × 9 interval equation is not enabled as a drug-dose calculator.

This sampled harmonized record is liposomal amphotericin. Conventional, liposomal and lipid-complex products are not mg-for-mg interchangeable; retain the source indication, immune status and infusion instructions.
Retain day-1 loading and once-daily maintenance together. Candidemia and esophageal courses differ; the source infusion rate must not exceed 1.1 mg/minute.
Retain all six oral doses over three days, food and source weight eligibility. Not a severe-malaria regimen; QT/CYP3A interactions and vomiting/repeat-dose instructions apply.
REYATAZ/ritonavir must retain both components and food. Treatment history, acid suppressants, interacting ART, formulation, pregnancy, hepatic and dialysis branches are not interchangeable.
PCP treatment 750-mg twice daily and prevention 1,500-mg once daily are different source branches. Food and adequate absorption are essential; severe PCP is not this treatment branch.
Preserve both components, adult/pediatric strength and complete treatment or travel-prophylaxis course. CrCl <30 excludes prophylaxis; treatment requires source-specific severe-renal review.
Preserve the complete adult day-1/day-2–5 course. Do not substitute a pediatric, sinusitis, single-dose STI or mycobacterial regimen; source QT/hepatic and interaction precautions apply.
CDC does not recommend amantadine for influenza treatment or prevention because of resistance. Its Parkinson/dyskinesia and extended-release regimens must not appear as antimicrobial doses.

Severe-malaria FDA/CDC source reference. The current FDA lookup has no harmonized artesunate card; no reference dose is substituted for a retrieved label. The source requires the initial IV sequence, reassessment and a complete follow-on oral course.

dosage_and_administration: 2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION Didanosine delayed-release capsules should be administered on an empty stomach. Didanosine delayed-release capsules should be swallowed intact. 2.1 Recommended Dosage (Adult and Pediatric Patients) The recommended total daily dose is based on body weight and is administered as one capsule given on a once-daily schedule as outlined in Table 1 . The recommended total daily dose to be administered once daily to pediatric patients weighing at least 20 kg who can swallow capsules is based on body weight (kg), consistent with the recommended adult dosing guidelines (see Table 1 ). Please consult the complete prescribing information for Didanosine Pediatric Powder for Oral Solution for dosage and administration of didanosine to pediatric patients weighing less than 20 kg or who can not swallow capsules. Table 1: Recommended Dosage (Adult and Pediatric Patients) Body Weight Dose 20 kg to less than 25 kg 200 mg once daily 25 kg to less than 60 kg 250 mg once daily at least 60 kg 400 mg once daily 2.2 Renal Impairment Dosing recommendations for didanosine delayed-release capsules are different for patients with renal impairment. Adult Patients In adult patients with impaired renal function, the dose of didanosine delayed-release capsules should be adjusted to compensate for the slower rate of elimination. The recommended doses and dosing intervals of didanosine delayed-release capsules in adult patients with renal insufficiency are presented in Table 2 . Table 2: Recommended Dosage in Patients with Renal Impairment by Body Weight Creatinine Clearance (mL/min) Dosage (mg) at least 60 kg less than 60 kg at least 60 400 once daily 250 once daily 30 to 59 200 once daily 125 once daily 10 to 29 125 once daily 125 once daily less than 10 125 once daily Pediatric Patients Urinary excretion is also a major route of elimination of didanosine in pediatric patients, therefore the clearance of didanosine may be altered in pediatric patients with renal impairment. Although there are insufficient data to recommend a specific dose adjustment of didanosine delayed-release capsules in this patient population, a reduction in the dose should be considered (see Table 2 ). Patients Requiring Continuous Ambulatory Peritoneal Dialysis (CAPD) or Hemodialysis For patients requiring CAPD or hemodialysis, follow dosing recommendations for patients with creatinine clearance of less than 10 mL/min, shown in Table 2 . It is not necessary to administer a supplemental dose of didanosine following hemodialysis. 2.3 Dose Adjustment Concomitant Therapy with Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate In patients who are also taking tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, a dose reduction of didanosine delayed-release capsules to 250 mg (adults weighing at least 60 kg with creatinine clearance of at least 60 mL/min) or 200 mg (adults weighing less than 60 kg with creatinine clearance of at least 60 mL/min) once daily taken together with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and a light meal (400 kcalories or less, 20% fat or less) or in the fasted state is recommended. The appropriate dose of didanosine delayed-release capsules coadministered with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate in patients with creatinine clearance of less than 60 mL/min has not been established [ see Drug Interactions ( 7 ) and Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 ) ]. Hepatic Impairment No dose adjustment is required in patients with hepatic impairment [ see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 ) and Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 ) ].

indications_and_usage: 1 INDICATIONS AND USAGE Didanosine delayed-release capsules, also known as ddI, in combination with other antiretroviral agents is indicated for the treatment of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-1 infection [ see Clinical Studies ( 14 ) ].
contraindications: 4 CONTRAINDICATIONS These recommendations are based on either drug interaction studies or observed clinical toxicities. 4.1 Allopurinol Coadministration of didanosine and allopurinol is contraindicated because systemic exposures of didanosine are increased, which may increase didanosine-associated toxicity [ see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 ) ]. 4.2 Ribavirin Coadministration of didanosine and ribavirin is contraindicated because exposures of the active metabolite of didanosine (dideoxyadenosine 5’-triphosphate) are increased. Fatal hepatic failure, as well as peripheral neuropathy, pancreatitis, and symptomatic hyperlactatemia/lactic acidosis have been reported in patients receiving both didanosine and ribavirin.

fixtures.sourcePassage: DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION Adults: Usual daily dose, 1 gram as 500 mg twice a day or 250 mg four times a day. Higher doses such as 500 mg four times a day may be required for severe infections or for those infections which do not respond to the smaller doses. For pediatric patients above eight years of age: Usual daily dose, 10 mg/lb to 20 mg/lb (25 mg/kg to 50 mg/kg) body weight divided in four equal doses. Administration of adequate amounts of fluid with the capsule formulation of tetracycline is recommended to wash down the drug and reduce the risk of esophageal irritation and ulceration (see ADVERSE REACTIONS ). Absorption of tetracycline is impaired by antacids containing aluminum, calcium or magnesium and preparations containing iron, zinc or sodium bicarbonate. Food and some dairy products also interfere with absorption. When used in streptococcal infections, therapy should be continued for 10 days. For treatment of brucellosis, 500 mg tetracycline four times a day for three weeks accompanied by streptomycin, 1 gram intramuscularly twice daily the first week and once daily the second week. For the treatment of syphilis in patients allergic to penicillin, the following dosage of tetracycline is recommended: early syphilis (less than one year’s duration), 500 mg four times a day for 15 days. Syphilis of more than one year’s duration (except neurosyphilis), 500 mg four times a day for 30 days. For treatment of gonorrhea, the recommended dose is 500 mg by mouth four times a day for seven days. Uncomplicated urethral, endocervical or rectal infections in adults caused by Chlamydia trachomatis : 500 mg, by mouth, four times a day for at least seven days. In cases of moderate to severe acne which, in the judgement of the clinician, require long-term treatment, the recommended initial dosage is 1 gram daily in divided doses. When improvement is noted, reduce dosage gradually to maintenance levels ranging from 125 mg to 500 mg daily. In some patients it may be possible to maintain adequate remission of lesions with alternate day or intermittent therapy. Tetracycline therapy of acne should augment the other standard measures known to be of value. Duration of long-term treatment which can safely be recommended has not been established (see WARNINGS and Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of Fertility ). fixtures.sourcePassage: 2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION Initial dose of 100 mg followed by 50 mg every 12 hours administered intravenously over approximately 30 to 60 minutes. ( 2.1 ) Severe hepatic impairment (Child Pugh C): Initial dose of 100 mg followed by 25 mg every 12 hours. ( 2.2 ) Obtain baseline blood coagulation parameters, including fibrinogen, and continue to monitor regularly during treatment with tigecycline for injection. ( 2.4 , 5.6 ) 2.1 Recommended Adult Dosage The recommended dosage regimen for tigecycline for injection is an initial dose of 100 mg, followed by 50 mg every 12 hours. Intravenous infusions of tigecycline for injection should be administered over approximately 30 to 60 minutes every 12 hours. The recommended duration of treatment with tigecycline for injection for complicated skin and skin structure infections or for complicated intra-abdominal infections is 5 to 14 days. The recommended duration of treatment with tigecycline for injection for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia is 7 to 14 days. The duration of therapy should be guided by the severity and site of the infection and the patient's clinical and bacteriological progress. 2.2 Dosage in Patients With Hepatic Impairment No dosage adjustment is warranted in patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment (Child Pugh A and Child Pugh B). In patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child Pugh C), the initial dose of tigecycline for injection should be 100 mg followed by a reduced maintenance dose of 25 mg every 12 hours. Patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child Pugh C) should be treated with caution and monitored for treatment response [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 ) and Use in Specific Populations ( 8.6 )] . 2.3 Dosage in Pediatric Patients The safety and efficacy of the proposed pediatric dosing regimens have not been evaluated due to the observed increase in mortality associated with tigecycline for injection in adult patients. Avoid use of tigecycline for injection in pediatric patients unless no alternative antibacterial drugs are available. Under these circumstances, the following doses are suggested: Pediatric patients aged 8 to 11 years should receive 1.2 mg/kg of tigecycline for injection every 12 hours intravenously to a maximum dose of 50 mg of tigecycline for injection every 12 hours. Pediatric patients aged 12 to 17 years should receive 50 mg of tigecycline for injection every 12 hours. The proposed pediatric doses of tigecycline for injection were chosen based on exposures observed in pharmacokinetic trials, which included small numbers of pediatric patients [see Use in Specific Populations ( 8.4 ) and Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 )] . There are no data to provide dosing recommendations in pediatric patients with hepatic impairment. 2.4 Monitoring of Blood Coagulation Parameters Obtain baseline blood coagulation parameters, including fibrinogen, and continue to monitor regularly during treatment with tigecycline for injection [see Warnings and Precautions (5.6)] . 2.5 Preparation and Administration Each vial of tigecycline for injection should be reconstituted with 5.3 mL of 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection, USP, 5% Dextrose Injection, USP, or Lactated Ringer's Injection, USP to achieve a concentration of 10 mg per mL of tigecycline. (Note: Each vial contains a 6% overage. Thus, 5 mL of reconstituted solution is equivalent to 50 mg of the drug.) The vial should be gently swirled until the drug dissolves. Reconstituted solution must be transferred and further diluted for intravenous infusion. Withdraw 5 mL of the reconstituted solution from the vial and add to a 100 mL intravenous bag for infusion (for a 100 mg dose, reconstitute two vials; for a 50 mg dose, reconstitute one vial). The maximum concentration in the intravenous bag should be 1 mg per mL. The reconstituted solution should be yellow to orange in color; if not, the solution should be discarded. Parenteral drug products should be inspected visually for particulate matter and discoloration (e.g., green or black) prior to administration. Once reconstituted, tigecycline for injection may be stored at room temperature (not to exceed 25ºC/77ºF) for up to 24 hours (up to 6 hours in the vial and the remaining time in the intravenous bag). If the storage conditions exceed 25ºC (77ºF) after reconstitution, tigecycline should be used immediately. Alternatively, tigecycline for injection mixed with 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection, USP or 5% Dextrose Injection, USP may be stored refrigerated at 2° to 8°C (36° to 46°F) for up to 48 hours following immediate transfer of the reconstituted solution into the intravenous bag. Tigecycline for injection may be administered intravenously through a dedicated line or through a Y-site. If the same intravenous line is used for sequential infusion of several drugs, the line should be flushed before and after infusion of tigecycline for injection with 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection, USP, 5% Dextrose Injection, USP or Lactated Ringer's Injection, USP. Injection should be made with an infusion solution compatible with tigecycline and with any other drug(s) administered via this common line. 2.6 Drug Compatibilities Compatible intravenous solutions include 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection, USP, 5% Dextrose Injection, USP, and Lactated Ringer's Injection, USP. When administered through a Y-site, tigecycline for injection is compatible with the following drugs or diluents when used with either 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection, USP or 5% Dextrose Injection, USP: amikacin, dobutamine, dopamine HCl, gentamicin, haloperidol, Lactated Ringer's, lidocaine HCl, metoclopramide, morphine, norepinephrine, piperacillin/tazobactam (EDTA formulation), potassium chloride, propofol, ranitidine HCl, theophylline, and tobramycin. 2.7 Drug Incompatibilities The following drugs should not be administered simultaneously through the same Y-site as tigecycline for injection: amphotericin B, amphotericin B lipid complex, diazepam, esomeprazole, and omeprazole.

Premature or Full-Term Neonates 1 Week of Age or Less: Up to 4 mg/kg/day may be administered in 2 equal doses every 12 hours. It is desirable to limit treatment to a short term. The usual duration of treatment is 7 to 10 days. A longer course of therapy may be necessary in difficult and complicated infections. In such cases, monitoring of renal, auditory, and vestibular functions is advised, because neurotoxicity is more likely to occur when treatment is extended longer than 10 days. Dosage in Patients with Cystic Fibrosis In patients with cystic fibrosis, altered pharmacokinetics may result in reduced serum concentration of aminoglycosides. Measurement of tobramycin serum concentration during treatment is especially important as a basis for determining appropriate dose. In patients with severe cystic fibrosis, an initial dosing regimen of 10 mg/kg/day in 4 equally divided doses is recommended. This dosing regimen is suggested only as a guide. The serum levels of tobramycin should be measured directly during treatment due to a wide interpatient variability. Administration for Patients with Impaired Renal Function Whenever possible, serum tobramycin concentrations should be monitored during therapy. Following a loading dose of 1 mg/kg, subsequent dosage in these patients must be adjusted, either with reduced doses administered at 8-hour intervals or with normal doses given at prolonged intervals. Both of these methods are suggested as guides to be used when serum levels of tobramycin cannot be measured directly. They are based on either the creatinine clearance or the serum creatinine of the patient, because these values correlate with the half-life of tobramycin. The dosage schedules derived from either method should be used in conjunction with careful clinical and laboratory observations of the patient and should be modified as necessary. Neither method should be used when dialysis is being performed. Reduced Dosage at 8-hour Intervals When the creatinine clearance rate is 70 mL or less per minute or when the serum creatinine value is known, the amount of the reduced dose can be determined by multiplying the normal dose from Table 1 by the percent of normal dose from the accompanying nomogram. An alternate rough guide for determining reduced dosage at 8-hour intervals (for patients whose steady-state serum creatinine values are known) is to divide the normally recommended dose by the patient's serum creatinine. Normal Dosage at Prolonged Intervals If the creatinine clearance rate is not available and the patient's condition is stable, a dosage frequency in hours for the dosage given in Table 1 can be determined by multiplying the patient's serum creatinine by 6. Dosage in Obese Patients The appropriate dose may be calculated by using the patient's estimated lean body weight plus 40% of the excess as the basic weight on which to figure mg/kg. Intramuscular Administration Tobramycin Injection, USP may be administered by withdrawing the appropriate dose directly from a vial. Tobramycin Sulfate in 0.9% Sodium Chloride is not intended for intramuscular administration. Intravenous Administration For intravenous administration, the usual volume of diluent (0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection or 5% Dextrose Injection) is 50 to 100 mL for adult doses. For pediatric patients, the volume of diluent should be proportionately less than for adults. The diluted solution usually should be infused over a period of 20 to 60 minutes. Infusion periods of less than 20 minutes are not recommended because peak serum levels may exceed 12 mcg/mL (see WARNINGS box). Tobramycin Injection, USP should not be physically premixed with other drugs but should be administered separately according to the recommended dose and route. Genital Herpes Initial Episode: The recommended dosage of valacyclovir tablets for treatment of initial genital herpes is 1 gram twice daily for 10 days. Therapy was most effective when administered within 48 hours of the onset of signs and symptoms. Recurrent Episodes: The recommended dosage of valacyclovir tablets for treatment of recurrent genital herpes is 500 mg twice daily for 3 days. Initiate treatment at the first sign or symptom of an episode. Suppressive Therapy: The recommended dosage of valacyclovir tablets for chronic suppressive therapy of recurrent genital herpes is 1 gram once daily in patients with normal immune function. In patients with a history of 9 or fewer recurrences per year, an alternative dose is 500 mg once daily. In HIV-1-infected patients with a CD4+ cell count greater than or equal to 100 cells/mm 3 , the recommended dosage of valacyclovir tablets for chronic suppressive therapy of recurrent genital herpes is 500 mg twice daily. Reduction of Transmission: The recommended dosage of valacyclovir tablets for reduction of transmission of genital herpes in patients with a history of 9 or fewer recurrences per year is 500 mg once daily for the source partner. Herpes Zoster The recommended dosage of valacyclovir tablets for treatment of herpes zoster is 1 gram 3 times daily for 7 days. Therapy should be initiated at the earliest sign or symptom of herpes zoster and is most effective when started within 48 hours of the onset of rash. 2.2 Pediatric Dosing Recommendations Cold Sores (Herpes Labialis) The recommended dosage of valacyclovir tablets for the treatment of cold sores in pediatric patients aged greater than or equal to 12 years is 2 grams twice daily for 1 day taken 12 hours apart. Therapy should be initiated at the earliest symptom of a cold sore (e.g., tingling, itching, or burning). Chickenpox The recommended dosage of valacyclovir tablets for treatment of chickenpox in immunocompetent pediatric patients aged 2 to less than 18 years is 20 mg/kg administered 3 times daily for 5 days. The total dose should not exceed 1 gram 3 times daily. Therapy should be initiated at the earliest sign or symptom [see Use in Specific Populations (8.4) , Clinical Pharmacology (12.3) , Clinical Studies (14.4) ]. 2.3 Extemporaneous Preparation of Oral Suspension Ingredients and Preparation per USP-NF Valacyclovir tablets 500 mg, cherry flavor, and Suspension Structured Vehicle USP-NF (SSV). Valacyclovir oral suspension (25 mg/mL or 50 mg/mL) should be prepared in lots of 100 mL. Instructions for Preparing Suspension at Time of Dispensing Prepare SSV according to the USP-NF. Using a pestle and mortar, grind the required number of valacyclovir tablets 500-mg until a fine powder is produced (5 valacyclovir tablets for 25-mg/mL suspension; 10 valacyclovir tablets for 50-mg/mL suspension). Gradually add approximately 5-mL aliquots of SSV to the mortar and triturate the powder until a paste has been produced. Ensure that the powder has been adequately wetted. Continue to add approximately 5-mL aliquots of SSV to the mortar, mixing thoroughly between additions, until a concentrated suspension is produced, to a minimum total quantity of 20 mL SSV and a maximum total quantity of 40 mL SSV for both the 25-mg/mL and 50-mg/mL suspensions. Transfer the mixture to a suitable 100-mL measuring flask. Transfer the cherry flavor The amount of cherry flavor added is as instructed by the suppliers of the cherry flavor. to the mortar and dissolve in approximately 5 mL of SSV. Once dissolved, add to the measuring flask. Rinse the mortar at least 3 times with approximately 5-mL aliquots of SSV, transferring the rinsing to the measuring flask between additions. Make the suspension to volume (100 mL) with SSV and shake thoroughly to mix. Transfer the suspension to an amber glass medicine bottle with a child-resistant closure. The prepared suspension should be labeled with the following information "Shake well before using. Store suspension between 2° to 8°C (36° to 46°F) in a refrigerator. Discard after 28 days." 2.4 Patients with Renal Impairment Dosage recommendations for adult patients with reduced renal function are provided in Table 1 [see Use in Specific Populations (8.5 , 8.6) , Clinical Pharmacology (12.3) ]. Data are not available for the use of valacyclovir tablets in pediatric patients with a creatinine clearance less than 50 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Table 1. During hemodialysis, the half-life of acyclovir after administration of valacyclovir tablets is approximately 4 hours. About one-third of acyclovir in the body is removed by dialysis during a 4-hour hemodialysis session. Peritoneal Dialysis There is no information specific to administration of valacyclovir tablets in patients receiving peritoneal dialysis. The effect of chronic ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) and continuous arteriovenous hemofiltration/dialysis (CAVHD) on acyclovir pharmacokinetics has been studied. The removal of acyclovir after CAPD and CAVHD is less pronounced than with hemodialysis, and the pharmacokinetic parameters closely resemble those observed in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) not receiving hemodialysis. Therefore, supplemental doses of valacyclovir tablets should not be required following CAPD or CAVHD.

Treatment of CMV Retinitis: Induction: The recommended dosage is 900 mg (two 450 mg tablets) taken orally twice a day for 21 days. Maintenance: Following induction treatment, or in adult patients with inactive CMV retinitis, the recommended dosage is 900 mg (two 450 mg tablets) taken orally once a day. Prevention of CMV Disease: For adult patients who have received a heart or kidney-pancreas transplant, the recommended dosage is 900 mg (two 450 mg tablets) taken orally once a day starting within 10 days of transplantation until 100 days post-transplantation. The recommended once daily dosage of valganciclovir tablets is based on body surface area (BSA) and creatinine clearance (CrCl) derived from a modified Schwartz formula, and is calculated using the equation below: Pediatric Dose (mg) = 7 x BSA x CrCl (calculated using a modified Schwartz formula). If the calculated Schwartz creatinine clearance exceeds 150 mL/min/1.73m 2 , then a maximum value of 150 mL/min/1.73m 2 should be used in the equation. The k values used in the modified Schwartz formula are based on pediatric patient age, as shown in Table 1 . All calculated doses should be rounded to the nearest 25 mg increment for the actual deliverable dose. If the calculated dose exceeds 900 mg, a maximum dose of 900 mg should be administered. Calculation for Estimated Creatinine Clearance in Adults 2.6 Handling and Disposal Caution should be exercised in the handling of valganciclovir tablets. Tablets should not be broken or crushed. Administer TYZAVAN by intravenous infusion over 60 minutes or greater to reduce the risk of infusion reactions ( 2.1 ) Recommended Dosage in Adult Patients with Normal Renal Function: 2 g divided either as 0.5 grams (g) every 6 hours or 1 g every 12 hours ( 2.2 ) Recommended Dosage in Pediatric Patients (1 Month and Older) with Normal Renal Function: 10 mg/kg per dose given every 6 hours ( 2.3 ) Recommended Dosage in Patients with Renal Impairment: See full prescribing information for recommended doses in patients with renal impairment ( 2.4 ) See full prescribing information for further important preparation and administration instructions ( 2.1, 2.5 ) 2.1 Important Administration Instructions If a dose of TYZAVAN is required that does not equal 500 mg, 750 mg, 1 g, 1.25 g, 1.5 g, 1.75 g or 2 g, this product is not recommended for use and an alternative formulation of vancomycin should be considered. TYZAVAN is intended for intravenous use only. TYZAVAN is not to be administered orally. To reduce the risk of infusion related adverse reactions, administer TYZAVAN by intravenous infusion over 60 minutes or greater [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1) and Adverse Reactions (6.1) ] . An infusion rate of 10 mg/min or less is associated with fewer infusion-related adverse reactions [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1) ] . Infusion related adverse reactions may occur, however, at any rate or concentration. Drug additives should not be made to this solution. TYZAVAN concentrations of no more than 5 mg/mL are recommended in adults and pediatric patients (1 month and older) [see Dosage and Administration (2.2) ] . See also age-specific recommendations [see Dosage and Administration (2.3) ] . Administer TYZAVAN by a secure intravenous route of administration to reduce the risk of local irritation and phlebitis reactions [see Warnings and Precautions (5.8) ] . Administer TYZAVAN prior to intravenous anesthetic agents to reduce the risk of infusion related adverse reactions [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1) ] . 2.2 Recommended Dosage in Adult Patients with Normal Renal Function The usual daily intravenous dosage of TYZAVAN is 2 grams (g) divided either as 500 mg every 6 hours or 1 g every 12 hours. Administer each dose by intravenous infusion over a period of 60 minutes or greater. Other patient factors, such as age or obesity, may call for modification of the usual intravenous daily dose. The initial daily dose should be no less than 15 mg/kg. 2.3 Recommended Dosage in Pediatric Patients (1 Month and Older) with Normal Renal Function If a dose of TYZAVAN is required that does not equal 500 mg, 750 mg, 1 g, 1.25 g, 1.5 g, 1.75 g or 2 g, this product is not recommended for use and an alternative formulation of vancomycin should be considered [see Use in Specific Populations (8.4) ] . Pediatric Patients (Aged 1 Month and Older) The usual intravenous dosage of TYZAVAN is 10 mg/kg per dose given every 6 hours. Each dose should be administered over a period of at least 60 minutes. Close monitoring of serum concentrations of vancomycin may be warranted in these patients. 2.4 Recommended Dosage in Adult Patients with Renal Impairment Dosage adjustment must be made in adult patients with renal impairment. The initial dose of TYZAVAN should be no less than 15 mg/kg in patients with any degree of renal impairment. In the elderly, greater dosage reductions than expected may be necessary because of decreased renal function. Measure trough vancomycin serum concentrations to guide therapy, especially in seriously ill patients with changing renal function. For functionally anephric patients, an initial dose of 15 mg/kg of body weight should be given to achieve prompt therapeutic serum concentration. A dose of 1.9 mg/kg/24 h should be given after the initial dose of 15 mg/kg. Measure vancomycin serum concentrations at 24 hours following the first dose to guide further intravenous therapy. 2.5 Administration and Preparation and Storage Instructions for TYZAVAN Administration Instructions TYZAVAN in transparent single-dose flexible bag is for intravenous administration only. Intermittent infusion is the recommended method of administration. TYZAVAN is a room temperature stable, ready-to-use drug product. Parenteral drug products should be inspected visually for particulate matter and discoloration prior to administration, whenever solution and container permit. Preparation for Intravenous Administration and Storage Instructions: 1. Remove the flexible bag from aluminum overpouch. 2. Check for minute leaks by squeezing the bag firmly. If leaks are detected, discard solution because sterility may be impaired. Leaks may be more readily detected by wrapping the bag with blotting paper or a tissue before squeezing. 3. Do not add supplemental medication. 4. Visually inspect the flexible bag. If the outlet port protector is damaged, detached, or not present, discard the flexible bag as solution path sterility may be impaired. If after visual inspection the solution is cloudy or if an insoluble precipitate is noted or if any seals are not intact, the flexible bag should be discarded. 5. The solution in the flexible bag remains chemically stable for 28 days at room temperature (15°C - 25°C (59°F – 77ºF)) after removal from the aluminum overpouch. Discard unused drug. 6. Suspend the flexible bag from eyelet support. 7. Remove protector from outlet port at bottom of flexible bag. 8. Attach administration set. Refer to complete directions accompanying set. 9. Use sterile equipment. Do not use flexible bags in series connections. Such use could result in an embolism due to residual air being drawn from the primary container before administration of the fluid from the secondary container is complete. 2.6 Incompatibilities for Intravenous Use Vancomycin solution has a low pH and may cause chemical or physical instability when it is mixed with other compounds. Mixtures of solutions of vancomycin and beta-lactam antibacterial drugs have been shown to be physically incompatible. The likelihood of precipitation increases with higher concentrations of vancomycin. It is recommended to adequately flush the intravenous lines between the administration of these antibacterial drugs.

If patient response is inadequate and the patient is able to tolerate the oral maintenance dose, the dose may be increased by 1 mg/kg (0.025 mL/kg) steps or 50 mg (1.25 mL) steps to a maximum of 350 mg (8.75 mL) every 12 hours. If patients are unable to tolerate the initial intravenous maintenance dose, reduce the dose by (1.25 mL) 1 mg/kg steps. If patients are unable to tolerate the oral maintenance dose, reduce the dose by 1 mg/kg (0.025 mL/kg) or 50 mg steps. There are no PK data to allow for dosage adjustment recommendations in patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class C). Duration of therapy should be based on the severity of the patient’s underlying disease, recovery from immunosuppression, and clinical response. Adult patients with baseline liver function tests (ALT, AST) of up to 5 times the upper limit of normal (ULN) were included in the clinical program. Dose adjustments are not necessary for adult patients with this degree of abnormal liver function, but continued monitoring of liver function tests for further elevations is recommended [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1) ]. It is recommended that the recommended voriconazole loading dose regimens be used, but that the maintenance dose be halved in adult patients with mild to moderate hepatic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh Class A and B) [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.3) ]. Voriconazole tablets have not been studied in adult patients with severe hepatic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh Class C) or in patients with chronic hepatitis B or chronic hepatitis C disease. Voriconazole tablets have been associated with elevations in liver function tests and with clinical signs of liver damage, such as jaundice. Voriconazole tablets should only be used in patients with severe hepatic impairment if the benefit outweighs the potential risk. Patients with hepatic impairment must be carefully monitored for drug toxicity. Pediatric Patients Dosage adjustment of voriconazole tablets in pediatric patients with hepatic impairment has not been established [see Use in Specific Populations (8.4) ]. 2.6 Dosage Modifications in Patients With Renal Impairment Adult Patients The pharmacokinetics of orally administered voriconazole tablets are not significantly affected by renal impairment. Therefore, no adjustment is necessary for oral dosing in patients with mild to severe renal impairment [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.3) ] . Oral voriconazole should be administered to these patients, unless an assessment of the benefit/risk to the patient justifies the use of intravenous voriconazole. Serum creatinine levels should be closely monitored in these patients, and, if increases occur, consideration should be given to changing to oral voriconazole therapy [see Warnings and Precautions (5.7) ]. Voriconazole and the intravenous vehicle, SBECD, are dialyzable. A 4-hour hemodialysis session does not remove a sufficient amount of voriconazole to warrant dose adjustment [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.3) ]. Pediatric Patients Dosage adjustment of voriconazole tablets in pediatric patients with renal impairment has not been established [see Use in Specific Populations (8.4) ] . 2.7 Dosage Adjustment When Co-Administered With Phenytoin or Efavirenz The maintenance dose of voriconazole should be increased when co-administered with phenytoin or efavirenz. Use the optimal method for titrating dosage [see Drug Interactions (7) and Dosage and Administration (2.3) ].

Prescribers should calculate the appropriate dose of zidovudine for each child based on body weight (kg) and should not exceed the recommended adult dose. Before prescribing zidovudine tablets, children should be assessed for the ability to swallow tablets. If a child is unable to reliably swallow a zidovudine tablet, the zidovudine syrup formulation should be prescribed. The recommended oral dosage in pediatric patients aged 4 weeks to less than 18 years and weighing greater than or equal to 4 kg is provided in Table 1. Zidovudine Syrup should be used to provide accurate dosage when tablets are not appropriate. Table 1. Recommended Pediatric Oral Dosage of Zidovudine Body Weight (kg) Total Daily Dose Dosage Regimen and Dose Twice Daily Three Times Daily 4 to <9 24 mg/kg/day 12 mg/kg 8 mg/kg ≥9 to <30 18 mg/kg/day 9 mg/kg 6 mg/kg ≥30 600 mg/day 300 mg 200 mg Alternatively, dosing for zidovudine can be based on body surface area (BSA) for each child. The recommended oral dose of zidovudine is 480 mg per m 2 per day in divided doses (240 mg per m2 twice daily or 160 mg per m 2 three times daily). In some cases the dose calculated by mg per kg will not be the same as that calculated by BSA. 2.3 Prevention of Maternal-Fetal HIV-1 Transmission The recommended dosage regimen for administration to pregnant women (greater than 14 weeks of pregnancy) and their neonates is: Maternal Dosing 100 mg orally 5 times per day until the start of labor [see Clinical Studies ( 14.3 )]. During labor and delivery, intravenous zidovudine should be administered at 2 mg per kg (total body weight) over 1 hour followed by a continuous intravenous infusion of 1 mg per kg per hour (total body weight) until clamping of the umbilical cord. Neonatal Dosing Start neonatal dosing within 12 hours after birth and continue through 6 weeks of age. Neonates unable to receive oral dosing may be administered zidovudine intravenously. See Table 2 for dosing recommendations. Table 2. Recommended Neonatal Dosages of Zidovudine Route Total Daily Dose Dose and Dosage Regimen Oral 8 mg/kg/day 2 mg/kg every 6 hours Intravenous 6 mg/kg/day 1.5 mg/kg infused over 30 minutes, every 6 hours Use an appropriate-sized syringe with 0.1-mL graduation to ensure accurate dosing of the syrup formulation in neonates. 2.4 Patients with Severe Anemia and/or Neutropenia Significant anemia (hemoglobin less than 7.5 g per dL or reduction greater than 25% of baseline) and/or significant neutropenia (granulocyte count less than 750 cells per mm 3 or reduction greater than 50% from baseline) may require a dose interruption until evidence of marrow recovery is observed [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )]. In patients who develop significant anemia, dose interruption does not necessarily eliminate the need for transfusion.
